## End Corporal Punishment

End Corporal Punishment acts as a catalyst for progress towards universal prohibition and elimination of corporal punishment of children. We support and analyse national progress, monitor legality and implementation worldwide, partner with organisations at all levels, and engage with human rights treaty body systems. End Corporal Punishment is hosted by the World Health Organization and supported by a multi-partner Advisory Committee.

LAST UPDATED March 2025
Also available online at www.endcorporalpunishment.org

The following table summarises the legal status of corporal punishment of children – and progress
towards achieving prohibition – in all states in all settings, the home, alternative care, day care, schools,
penal institutions and as a sentence for crime. Governments are increasingly enacting laws to prohibit
this form of violence against children. As at March 2025, 68 states have achieved prohibition in all
settings; governments of at least 25 other states have expressed a commitment to enacting full
prohibition. Draft legislation that would achieve prohibition in all or some settings is under discussion in
some states. With the exception of alternative care and day care, which include those forms of care
most closely linked with the legal duties and obligations of parents, the majority of states have
prohibited corporal punishment of children outside the family home, but there is much still to be done.
End Corporal Punishment offers technical support and advice on all aspects of law reform to achieve
prohibition and publishes a number of useful resources free of charge  – please see
www.endcorporalpunishment.org or email vohitos@who.int
Assessing global progress towards prohibition is a complex task. When a state reforms the law to
prohibit corporal punishment in the home, the legislation must be closely examined to ensure there are
no legal defences for its use by parents/carers (such as a “right of correction” or a right to administer
“reasonable” punishment), and that it prohibits all for  ms of corporal punishment, however light. The
Global Initiative also seeks official confirmation from governments and other sources that the new law
is unequivocally interpreted as prohibiting all corporal punishment in childrearing.
With regard to settings outside the home, in many states legislation explicitly prohibits corporal
punishment in schools and other institutions. In some states, the illegality of corporal punishment is
based on particular combinations of criminal laws on assault and the absence of a legal defence,
together with other legislation protecting children in the setting and relevant case law, etc.
Alternatively, there may be a high-level court judgment which makes corporal punishment unlawful but
which has yet to be confirmed in legislation. Of states in which corporal punishment is lawful in schools
or other institutions, some simply lack legislation prohibiting corporal punishment and some explicitly
authorise its use in those settings. There are also states that have prohibited corporal punishment in
some but not all aspects of a setting (e.g. prohibiting it only in primary schools). The table illustrates
some of the complexities: for full details see the individual country reports at
www.endcorporalpunishment.org; to provide us with further information please email vohitos@who.int

Also available online at www.endcorporalpunishment.org

The following table summarises the legal status of corporal punishment of children – and progress
towards achieving prohibition – in all states in all settings, the home, alternative care, day care, schools,
penal institutions and as a sentence for crime. Governments are increasingly enacting laws to prohibit
this form of violence against children. As at March 2025, 68 states have achieved prohibition in all
settings; governments of at least 25 other states have expressed a commitment to enacting full
prohibition. Draft legislation that would achieve prohibition in all or some settings is under discussion in
some states. With the exception of alternative care and day care, which include those forms of care
most closely linked with the legal duties and obligations of parents, the majority of states have
prohibited corporal punishment of children outside the family home, but there is much still to be done.
End Corporal Punishment offers technical support and advice on all aspects of law reform to achieve
prohibition and publishes a number of useful resources free of charge  – please see
www.endcorporalpunishment.org or email vohitos@who.int
Assessing global progress towards prohibition is a complex task. When a state reforms the law to
prohibit corporal punishment in the home, the legislation must be closely examined to ensure there are
no legal defences for its use by parents/carers (such as a “right of correction” or a right to administer
“reasonable” punishment), and that it prohibits all for  ms of corporal punishment, however light. The
Global Initiative also seeks official confirmation from governments and other sources that the new law
is unequivocally interpreted as prohibiting all corporal punishment in childrearing.
With regard to settings outside the home, in many states legislation explicitly prohibits corporal
punishment in schools and other institutions. In some states, the illegality of corporal punishment is
based on particular combinations of criminal laws on assault and the absence of a legal defence,
together with other legislation protecting children in the setting and relevant case law, etc.
Alternatively, there may be a high-level court judgment which makes corporal punishment unlawful but
which has yet to be confirmed in legislation. Of states in which corporal punishment is lawful in schools
or other institutions, some simply lack legislation prohibiting corporal punishment and some explicitly
authorise its use in those settings. There are also states that have prohibited corporal punishment in
some but not all aspects of a setting (e.g. prohibiting it only in primary schools). The table illustrates
some of the complexities: for full details see the individual country reports at
www.endcorporalpunishment.org; to provide us with further information please email vohitos@who.int

prohibition. Thirty-nine states have prohibited corporal punishment in all alternative care
settings, 40 in day care; all 54 states have prohibited corporal punishment in schools, in penal
institutions and as a sentence for crime.

The **legality of corporal punishment of children** varies by country. [Corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_the_home "Corporal punishment in the home") of minor children by parents or adult guardians, which is intended to cause physical pain, has been traditionally legal in nearly all countries unless explicitly outlawed. According to a 2014 estimate by [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch"), "Ninety percent of the world's children live in countries where corporal punishment and other physical violence against children is still legal".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-HRW-1) Many countries' laws provide for a defence of "reasonable chastisement" against charges of assault and other crimes for parents using corporal punishment. This defence is ultimately derived from [English law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_law "English law").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-2) As of 2026, only one ([France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")) [permanent member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") along with three (adding [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan")) of seven [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") members and seven (adding [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") and [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea")) of the 20 [G20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G20 "G20") member states have banned the use of corporal punishment against children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Gershoff2017-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-4)

### Argentina

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Argentina")]

Banned in 1813, [school corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment "School corporal punishment") was re-legalised in 1817 and punishments by physical pain lasted until the 1980s. The instruments were [rebenques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebenque "Rebenque"), [slappings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slapping_(strike) "Slapping (strike)") in the face and others.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-19) All corporal punishment was prohibited by a law in 2014 which came into force in January 2016.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-20)

### Australia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Australia")]

In [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), corporal punishment of minors in the home is legal, provided it is "reasonable".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-22) Corporal punishment in public schools is illegal in all states, and in private schools it is only allowed in Queensland.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-24) Parents who act unreasonably may be committing an assault.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-26) The Australian state of [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania "Tasmania") is continuing to review the state's laws on the matter, and may seek to ban the use of corporal punishment by parents. The matter is also under review in other Australian states. A 2002 public opinion survey suggested the majority view was in support of retaining parents' right to smack with the open hand but not with an implement,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-27) although as of 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit), there are no laws against using an implement in any state or territory. In New South Wales, S61AA of the Crimes Act (1900) allows a parent a defence of lawful correction.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-28) In New South Wales, one specifically cannot smack a child on the head or neck, and the child cannot be more than briefly harmed or bruised.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-29)

### Austria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Austria")]

School corporal punishment was explicitly prohibited in Austria in 1974. In 1977, corporal punishment in the home was outlawed by removing the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code that stated that parents who have used "reasonable punishment" of their children shall not be punished for assault. On 15 March 1989, corporal punishment of children became explicitly banned through a new law stating that "using violence and inflicting physical or mental suffering is unlawful".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-30)

### Belarus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Belarus")]

Corporal punishment in schools was banned in Belarus during the Soviet era, however it was decriminalized after its authoritarian president [Alexander Lukashenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Lukashenko "Alexander Lukashenko") took power in 1994. It is only permitted for male students older than 14. It cannot be inflicted on girls. School beltings are rare in major cities and remain much more common in rural areas, where parents tend to raise their children in more conservative manners. In 2018, Lukashenko rejected the bill that would have outlawed corporal punishments for minors both in educational facilities and at home, arguing that he himself belted his children in their adolescence to discipline them.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Canada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Canada")]

In [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), parents may use physical force to discipline their children, including spanking, but there are several restrictions.

Section 43 of the [_Criminal Code_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Code_(Canada) "Criminal Code (Canada)") provides that parents may use "reasonable" force as a form of discipline.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-31) The constitutionality of this provision was challenged in the courts, on the basis that it infringed the rights of children, contrary to three sections of the _[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Charter\_of\_Rights\_and\_Freedoms "Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms")_: the right to security of the person, protected by [section 7 of the _Charter_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_7_of_the_Canadian_Charter_of_Rights_and_Freedoms "Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms"); the right to be free from cruel and unusual treatment and punishment, protected by [section 12 of the _Charter_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_12_of_the_Canadian_Charter_of_Rights_and_Freedoms "Section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms"); and the right to equality (specifically, age), protected by [section 15 of _Charter_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_15_of_the_Canadian_Charter_of_Rights_and_Freedoms "Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms"). In 2004, the [Supreme Court of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Canada "Supreme Court of Canada") dismissed the constitutional challenge on all grounds, on a 6–3 split, in _[Canadian Foundation for Children, Youth and the Law v. Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Foundation\_for\_Children,\_Youth\_and\_the\_Law\_v.\_Canada\_(Attorney\_General) "Canadian Foundation for Children, Youth and the Law v. Canada (Attorney General)")_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-32)

In upholding section 43, the majority of the Court provided considerable guidance to the interpretation of the provision. The majority held that the person administering the discipline must be a parent or legal guardian, or in some cases, a school teacher (i.e. non-parental relatives such as grandparents, aunts, or uncles, as well as babysitters and other caretakers, are banned from spanking); that the force must be used "by way of correction" (sober, reasoned uses of force that address the actual behaviour of the child and are designed to restrain, control or express some symbolic disapproval of his or her behaviour), that the child must be capable of benefiting from the correction (i.e. not under the age of 2 or over 12), and that the use of force must be "reasonable under the circumstances", meaning that it results neither in harm nor in the prospect of bodily harm. Punishment involving slaps or blows to the head is harmful, the Court held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-33) Use of any implement other than a bare hand is illegal and hitting a child in anger or in retaliation for something a child did is not considered reasonable and is against the law. The Court defined "reasonable" as force that would have a "transitory and trifling" impact on the child. For example, spanking or slapping a child so hard that it leaves a mark that lasts for several hours would not be considered "transitory and trifling".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-34)

Among the recommendations of the [Truth and Reconciliation Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_and_Reconciliation_Commission_(Canada) "Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Canada)"), formed to redress the legacy of the [Canadian Indian residential school system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Indian_residential_school_system "Canadian Indian residential school system"), is a call to repeal Section 43 of the Criminal Code.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-35)

### Colombia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Colombia")]

On 23 March 2021, the [Senate of Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Colombia "Senate of Colombia") unanimously voted to approve a bill that prohibits physical punishment, cruel, humiliating, or degrading acts, and violence as forms of correctional approaches for the upbringing of children and adolescents in Colombia.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-36)

### Czech Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Czech Republic")]

Until 2026, the Czech Republic had remained the only country in the European Union that does not outlaw child corporal punishment or plan to introduce such a law.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-37) On July 17, 2025, the president signed an amendment to the Civil Code, making corporal punishment of children explicitly prohibited by law, beginning January 1, 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-cz-16)

### Denmark

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Denmark")]

Corporal punishment in schools in Denmark became explicitly prohibited in 1967 and in 1985, parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children became outlawed through a new law which required parents "to protect their child from physical and psychological violence and other humiliating treatment".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-39) However, the law was believed to still support corporal punishment as there was a controversy whether the law permitted parents to punish their children physically or otherwise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-40) Therefore, after several years of debate, a new, clearer law came into force on 28 May 1997, providing that "_The child has right to care and security. It must be treated with respect for its person and must not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment_".

Denmark's [autonomous territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_administrative_division "Autonomous administrative division"), the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands") and [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), banned corporal punishment of children in 2007 and 2016, respectively.

### Finland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Finland")]

School corporal punishment was banned in 1914.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-41) Parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was outlawed in 1969 when the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, stating that a "petty assault" was not punishable if committed by parents or others who exercise their right to chastise a child, was removed. In 1983, corporal punishment of children was explicitly banned.

### France

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: France")]

In the [Napoleonic era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_era "Napoleonic era") parents were explicitly allowed to physically punish their children. Spanking was previously popular, with 85% of French parents admitting to using it. However, in 2019, the National Assembly approved a bill introducing a complete ban on all forms of physical punishment of children and required mayors officiating at civil weddings to remind couples that violence against children is unlawful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-auto-7) The law makes corporal punishment a civil offense, not a criminal one.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-42)

### Germany

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Germany")]

[School corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment "School corporal punishment") was prohibited in [East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany "East Germany") (which became part of the Federal Republic of [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") at the [German reunification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification "German reunification") on 3 October 1990). In the Federal Republic ([West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany") before reunification), it was prohibited at different times in its different [states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_of_Germany "States of Germany") between 1975 and 1983.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-43)

In the Federal Republic of Germany, in 1980 it became prohibited for parents to educate their children with "degrading measures" (it was not clear exactly what "degrading" meant), of which the common interpretation was that [corporal punishment of children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_the_home "Corporal punishment in the home") was still permitted as long as it was not "degrading". On 1 July 1998, corporal punishment was outlawed through a new law stating that "Degrading educational measures, especially physical and psychological maltreatment, are inadmissible"; the common interpretation of that law was that parents still had some right to use corporal punishment on their children. In November 2000, that law was replaced with a new more clear and strict law stating that "_Children have right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological violence and other degrading educational measures are inadmissible._"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-45)

### Greece

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Greece")]

The 2006 enacted Law 3500/06 on the treatment of domestic violence prohibits the use of physical violence against a minor as a means of punishment in the context of his upbringing, with the explicit clarification - in the explanatory memorandum - that corporal punishment is not included. to the permissible penitentiary measures of article 1518 of the Civil Code and that its use entails for the parents the consequences of the bad exercise of parental care.

Specifically, Article 4 provides that physical violence against minors as a means of punishment in the context of their upbringing brings about the consequences of Article 1532 of the Civil Code. The explanatory memorandum to this article states, among other things: “The regulation of Article 4 makes it clear that corporal punishment against children is not included in the permissible punishment measures of Article 1518 of the Civil Code in accordance with modern pedagogical views. It constitutes a case of poor exercise of custody and for this reason brings about the application of article 1532 of the Civil Code. According to this article, in such a case, the court may order any appropriate measure. "Any act of inflicting pain or physical discomfort on a minor should be treated as physical violence, with the aim of punishing or controlling his behavior."

### Ireland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Ireland")]

In Ireland, all forms of corporal punishment of children have been definitively outlawed since the passing of the [Children First Act 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_First_Act_2015 "Children First Act 2015").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46)[Law in the Republic of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_in_the_Republic_of_Ireland "Law in the Republic of Ireland") inherited the pre-independence [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law "Common law") and statutes modelled on [English law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_law "English law"). These included allowance under common law of "physical [chastisement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chastisement "Chastisement")" by teachers, and under the [Children Act 1908](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_Act_1908 "Children Act 1908") ([8 Edw. 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8_Edw._7 "8 Edw. 7"). c. 67) of "reasonable chastisement" by parents and those _[in loco parentis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_loco\_parentis "In loco parentis")_. [School corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment "School corporal punishment") was prohibited in 1982 by an administrative decision of [John Boland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boland_(Fine_Gael_politician) "John Boland (Fine Gael politician)"), the [Minister for Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Education_and_Youth "Minister for Education and Youth").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-dail20151021-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-48) Teachers were not liable to criminal prosecution until 1997, when the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law") allowing physical chastisement was explicitly abolished.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-49) The Children Act 2001 repealed the 1908 act but, except in children detention schools, did not explicitly prohibit corporal punishment;[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-it1512623-51) the common-law defence of "reasonable chastisement" remained available to parents facing a charge of assault.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-it1512623-51)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46) In response to a complaint filed with the [European Committee of Social Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Committee_of_Social_Rights "European Committee of Social Rights"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-52) the defence was abolished under the Children First Act 2015.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-53)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-dail20151021-47)

### Italy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Italy")]

School corporal punishment became prohibited in 1928. In 1996, the [Supreme Court of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Italy "Supreme Court of Italy") ruled that in domestic settings, physical punishment is no longer an acceptable way to discipline children.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-54) However, that is still yet to be confirmed in legislation.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-55)

### India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: India")]

In India, corporal punishment is banned in schools, daycare and alternative child care institutions. However, there are no prohibitions of it at home. The National Policy for Children 2013 states that in education, the state shall “ensure no child is subjected to any physical punishment or mental harassment” and “promote positive engagement to impart discipline so as to provide children with a good learning experience”. Corporal punishment is prohibited in schools in the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 (RTE Act). Article 17 states: “(1) No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment. (2) Whoever contravenes the provisions of sub-section (1) shall be liable to disciplinary action under the service rules applicable to such person.” Guidance (”Advisory for Eliminating Corporal Punishment in Schools under Section 35(1) of the RTE Act 2009”) which sets out the national law relevant to corporal punishment in schools, the international human rights standards, steps that may be taken to promote positive child development and not resorting to corporal punishment, and the role of national bodies in implementing the RTE Act, stating: “This advisory should be used by the State Governments/UT Administrations to ensure that appropriate State/school level guidelines on prevention of corporate punishment and appropriate redressal of any complaints, are framed, disseminated, acted upon and monitored.”[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-57)

According to Vasudev Sharma, the executive director of Child Rights Trust, [Bengaluru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengaluru "Bengaluru"), "Many teachers hauled up for corporal punishment claim protection under Sections 88 and 89 of the [Indian Penal Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Penal_Code "Indian Penal Code") (IPC) saying they were taking action in good faith." Section 88 protects "Acts not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person’s benefit" and Section 89 "act[s] done in good faith for benefit of child or insane person, by or by consent of guardian."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-58)

### Israel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Israel")]

On 25 January 2000, the [Supreme Court of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Israel "Supreme Court of Israel") issued the landmark _Plonit_ decision ruling that "corporal punishment of children by their parents is never educational", "always causes serious harm to the children" and "is indefensible".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel1-59) This decision repealed section 7 of article 27 of the Civil Wrongs Ordinance 1944, which provided a defence for the use of corporal punishment in childrearing, and stated that "the law imposes an obligation on state authorities to intervene in the family unit and to protect the child when necessary, including from his parents."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel2-60) As a result, all kinds of physical discipline against children were automatically banned through the country, as confirmed by multiple subsequent court rulings.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel3-61)

### Nepal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Nepal")]

In September 2018, Nepal adopted the "Children's act 2018" which criminalises corporal punishment of children in all settings.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-The_Himalayan_Times_2018-62)

### New Zealand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: New Zealand")]

The [Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_(Substituted_Section_59)_Amendment_Act_2007 "Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007") or "anti-smacking bill" was introduced as a member's bill by Green Party Member of Parliament [Sue Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Bradford "Sue Bradford") in 2005 passed on its third reading on 16 May 2007 by 113 votes to eight.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-64)

The [2009 New Zealand citizens-initiated referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_New_Zealand_citizens-initiated_referendum "2009 New Zealand citizens-initiated referendum") posed the question: "Should a smack as part of good parental correction be a criminal offence in New Zealand?"[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-65) 87.4% of votes answered "No". The referendum was non-binding and did not lead to a change in the law. It was noted at the time that "the wording of the proposition was misleading and ambiguous".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-66)

### Norway

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Norway")]

School corporal punishment was explicitly prohibited in 1936. In 1972, an 1891 law that gave parents some right to use corporal punishment of their children was removed from the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, which made corporal punishment of children unlawful and punishable as assault. In order to clarify that violence towards children is not allowed, an explicit ban on corporal punishment of children came into force in 1987.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-67)

However, the [Supreme Court of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Norway "Supreme Court of Norway") ruled in 2005 that a light "careful slap" applied immediately after the "offence" was still allowed.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-69) The legislature abolished this in 2010, and the current law is that any violence against children, including "careful slaps", is prohibited.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-70)

### Philippines

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Philippines")]

Legislation to ban corporal punishment against children has been proposed in the Philippines. In 2023 under the [19th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_Congress_of_the_Philippines "19th Congress of the Philippines"), House Bills 8306 and House Bill 1269 were filed to penalize individuals practicing corporal punishment.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-71)

### Poland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Poland")]

In 1783, Poland became the world's first country to outlaw school corporal punishment and the first Slavic country to outlaw corporal punishment. According to article 40 in the 1997 [Constitution of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Poland "Constitution of Poland"), "_No one may be subjected to torture or cruel, [inhuman, or degrading treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inhuman,\_or\_degrading\_treatment "Inhuman, or degrading treatment") or punishment. The application of corporal punishment shall be prohibited._"[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-72) However, there was a controversy whether parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was supported by law or not, until 2010, when it became explicitly prohibited.

### South Africa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: South Africa")]

Common-law precedent in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") held that a parent may "inflict moderate and reasonable chastisement" on a child.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-ecp-za-73) The [judicial corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_corporal_punishment "Judicial corporal punishment") of juveniles was forbidden by the [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_South_Africa "Constitutional Court of South Africa") in the 1995 case _[S v Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S\_v\_Williams\_(1995) "S v Williams (1995)")_. [Corporal punishment in schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools "Corporal punishment in schools") was banned by the [South African Schools Act, 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Schools_Act,_1996 "South African Schools Act, 1996"), and the application of that ban to private religious schools was upheld by the Constitutional Court in the case of _[Christian Education South Africa v Minister of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian\_Education\_South\_Africa\_v\_Minister\_of\_Education "Christian Education South Africa v Minister of Education")_.

In 2013, the [Department of Social Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Social_Development_(South_Africa) "Department of Social Development (South Africa)") prepared legislation to prohibit corporal punishment in the home.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-74) In 2017 a decision by the [Gauteng High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauteng_High_Court "Gauteng High Court") held that corporal punishment in the home was unlawful,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-parent24.com-75) and that decision was confirmed for the whole country by the Constitutional Court in the 2019 case _[Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom\_of\_Religion\_South\_Africa\_v\_Minister\_of\_Justice\_and\_Constitutional\_Development "Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development")_.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-76)

### South Korea

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: South Korea")]

In South Korea, until 2021, article 915 of the Civil Act 1958 provided adults the "right to take disciplinary action". Laws against violence and abuse were not generally interpreted as prohibiting corporal punishment of children.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-77) In January 2021, article 915 was fully repealed and South Korea become the 62nd country in the world to ban all kinds of corporal punishment against children.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-korea1-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-korea2-79)

### Spain

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Spain")]

All kinds of corporal punishment of children including "smacking" were banned by the [1st Zapatero government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_government_of_Jos%C3%A9_Luis_Rodr%C3%ADguez_Zapatero "First government of José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero") in December 2007.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain0-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain1-81) School corporal punishment had been prohibited in 1985 by [another Social-Democratic government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_government_of_Felipe_Gonz%C3%A1lez "First government of Felipe González").

In June 2021, the [Spanish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortes_Generales "Cortes Generales") passed a new, pioneering child and adolescent protection law against all kinds of violence or abuse. It was championed by the British-Spanish pianist [James Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Rhodes_(pianist) "James Rhodes (pianist)") and the [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics") party [Unidas Podemos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unidas_Podemos "Unidas Podemos"), but eventually supported by all political groups in Parliament except [Vox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vox_(political_party) "Vox (political party)"). A Code of Minors is also being drafted.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain3-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain4-83)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Spain0-80)

### Sweden

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Sweden")]

See also: [Corporal punishment in the home §The 1979 Swedish ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_the_home#The_1979_Swedish_ban "Corporal punishment in the home")

Sweden was the world's first nation to outlaw all corporal punishment of children in 1966, when the law that permitted parents to use corporal punishment of their children became removed and fully replaced with the constitution of assault under the Penal Code; however, even though the law no longer supported parents' right to use physical punishment of their children, it was believed to still be permitted (as there was no explicit ban). School corporal punishment was already banned since 1958.

On 1 July 1979, Sweden became the world's first nation to explicitly ban corporal punishment of children, through an amendment to the Parenthood and Guardianship Code which stated, "Children are entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. Children are to be treated with respect for their person and individuality and may not be subjected to corporal punishment or any other humiliating treatment." In Parliament - the law was supported 259 to 6 with 3 abstentions.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Modig-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-SocialSciences-86) Corporal punishment in Sweden is not seen as a separate legal issue - but is handled according to the criteria for assault.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Durrant_1996-84)

One thing that helped pave the way for the ban was a 1971 murder case where a 3-year-old girl was beaten to death by her stepfather. The case shook the general public and preventing child abuse became a political hot topic for years to come.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-87)

It is estimated that approximately 5% of Swedish children continue to be illegally spanked, however, in addition to being unlawful, physical punishment of children is now considered socially unacceptable.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-88)

### Switzerland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Switzerland")]

On September 26, 2025, [both chambers of the Federal Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Assembly_(Switzerland) "Federal Assembly (Switzerland)") approved the inclusion of "non-violent parenting" in Swiss law. The law forbids "physical punishment and other forms of degrading treatment". The Federal Council is to decide at the beginning of 2026 when the new law start to take effect.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-ch-17)

### Turkey

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Turkey")]

#### Simple form

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Simple form")]

In [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), corporal punishment is unlawful, considered [assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault "Assault"),[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-89) and is punishable by imprisonment for a term not less than 1 year and not more than 3 years if none of the special cases below occur.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-90)

#### Special cases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Special cases")]

If the courts deem that any one of:

*   "the victim is physically or psychologically unable to defend themselves",
*   the victim is the child of the perpetrator, or
*   a weapon (which is defined to include "anything used in defense or offense"[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-91)) is used in the act is true, the punishment is increased by half of the original amount.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-92) If the courts deem that the perpetrator acted in a "fiendish" way, the punishment is increased to twice the original amount.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-93) If either one or both of these are true, it is said that the act was "egregious".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-94)

If the victim suffers, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:

*   persistent weakness in any of their senses or organs,
*   persistent hardship in speaking,
*   a permanent mark on their face, or
*   a danger to their life,

the punishment determined above is increased to twice its final amount (determined above).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-95) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 3 years, or 5 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-96)

Alternatively, if the victim, as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, any one of:

*   begins to suffer from an illness for which there is no cure, or, enters a [persistent vegetative state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persistent_vegetative_state "Persistent vegetative state"),
*   suffers a complete loss of function to one of their senses or organs,
*   loses the ability to speak or to reproduce, or
*   a permanent change to their face,

the punishment determined above is increased to thrice its final amount (determined above).[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-97) However, the final punishment if these occur, cannot be less than imprisonment for a term of 5 years, or 8 years if the act was deemed to be "egregious".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-98)

If the victim suffers a broken bone as a result of corporal punishment being used on them, the courts may increase the final punishment by up to half its original amount, depending on the vitality of the broken bone to daily life.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-99)

If the victim dies as a result of corporal punishment being used on them but the act does not meet the criteria for [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder "Murder"), the final punishment must be imprisonment for a term not less than 8 years and not more than 12 years. If the act was found to be "egregious", the term of imprisonment must be between 12 and 18 years.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-100)

### United Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: United Kingdom")]

In the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), the law regarding domestic corporal punishment varies by jurisdiction.

#### England and Wales

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: England and Wales")]

Main article: [Legality of corporal punishment in England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_corporal_punishment_in_England_and_Wales "Legality of corporal punishment in England and Wales")

##### England

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: England")]

Criminal law has a general prohibition against [common assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_assault "Common assault") and [battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_(crime)#United_Kingdom "Battery (crime)"), but corporal punishment is legal through tradition and an implicit common law justification/[defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affirmative_defense "Affirmative defense") (_R v Hopley_ 2F&F 202, 1860[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-101)) to such charges for parents striking their children in the context of "lawful correction" where the act is "moderate and reasonable". The [Children Act 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_Act_2004 "Children Act 2004")[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-102) effectively provides a statutory definition of 'immoderate' by disallowing this justification for any act of punishment inflicting injuries or effects that amount to strangulation, wounding, [actual bodily harm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_occasioning_actual_bodily_harm "Assault occasioning actual bodily harm") (ABH), or any act considered "cruelty to persons under sixteen" in violation of the [Children and Young Persons Act 1933](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_and_Young_Persons_Act_1933 "Children and Young Persons Act 1933"), and was described at implementation as criminalising "visible bruising"[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-103) and rendering lesser injuries (comparable to "not serious" common assault) implicitly lawful/defensible. At the time, the [Crown Prosecution Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prosecution_Service "Crown Prosecution Service") (CPS) produced a charging standard unlawfully asserting the age of the victim may be considered an aggravating factor in deciding if the offence charged would be indefensible serious assault occasioning ABH rather than (implicitly defensible) common assault and erroneously asserted that any injuries more than "temporary reddening of the skin" or "marks" could be charged as ABH; this had no legal basis and was withdrawn in 2011. Standards now correctly require evidence of injuries that are "serious" and where a "sentence clearly in excess of six months' imprisonment ought to be available"[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-104) (as legal precedent requires/demands injuries "must, no doubt, be more than merely transient and trifling" now being interpreted as "more than common assault") to warrant an indefensible criminal charge of ABH.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-105)

Utilising the unlawful threshold, the courts of England and Wales have convicted parents on the basis that their acts amounted to ABH and were therefore unlawful, yet have passed sentences less than six months, contrary to the requirement of more than six months; police and social services also continue to use the long-withdrawn assertions of the CPS, leading to some parents or others acting _[in loco parentis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_loco\_parentis "In loco parentis")_ being criminalised (often by police cautions for lesser common assault on a position of guilt to ABH) or investigated for causing minor injuries that did not amount to ABH in law.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-106)[_[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research#Primary,\_secondary\_and\_tertiary\_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")_][[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-107)

The total abolition of corporal punishment has been discussed.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-108) In a 2004 poll by the advocacy group Children are Unbeatable!, 71% of respondents supported giving children the same protection against battery as adults if it "would not lead to parents being prosecuted for trivial or minor acts of physical punishment".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-109) In a 2006 survey, 80% of the population said they believed in smacking, and 73% said that they believed that any ban would cause a sharp deterioration in children's behaviour. Seven out of ten parents said they themselves use corporal punishment.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-110) In a 2012 poll conducted by [Angus Reid Public Opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_Reid_Public_Opinion "Angus Reid Public Opinion"), 63% of Britons voiced opposition to banning parents in the UK from smacking their children.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-111)

##### Wales

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Wales")]

The Welsh Government introduced a Bill to abolish the defence of reasonable punishment in Wales.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-112) On 20 March 2020 the Welsh Assembly passed the [Children (Abolition of Defence of Reasonable Punishment) (Wales) Act 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_(Abolition_of_Defence_of_Reasonable_Punishment)_(Wales)_Act_2020 "Children (Abolition of Defence of Reasonable Punishment) (Wales) Act 2020").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-113) This change in the law gives children the same legal protection from assault as adults.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-114) On 21 March 2022 the “smacking ban” came into force in Wales, making corporal punishment of children officially illegal.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-115)

#### Scotland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Scotland")]

In Scotland, since 2003 it has been unlawful to punish a child using any implement, or to strike them upon the head and corporal punishment of children under the age of 3 is unlawful.

In 2017, the Scottish Government confirmed it would support a member's bill to ban all corporal punishment completely. In 2019, the Scottish Parliament passed the [Children (Equal Protection from Assault) (Scotland) Act 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_(Equal_Protection_from_Assault)_(Scotland)_Act_2019 "Children (Equal Protection from Assault) (Scotland) Act 2019"), parts of which commenced immediately, while other parts commenced 1 year later.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-116)

#### Northern Ireland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Northern Ireland")]

In Northern Ireland, laws regarding corporal punishment are similar to England. It is unlawful to hit a child upon the head or use an implement.

#### Jersey

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Jersey")]

In Jersey, corporal punishment was banned in 2020 by the passage of the Children and Education (Amendment) (Jersey) Law 2020.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-117)

### United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: United States")]

Main article: [Corporal punishment of minors in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_of_minors_in_the_United_States "Corporal punishment of minors in the United States")

Corporal punishment of children by parents is legal to some extent in all fifty of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), and is explicitly legal according to the state laws of all 50 states. Social acceptance is generally high, through allowances made for "moderate physical discipline" (using this or similar language) in most states' laws regarding [assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault "Assault"), [criminal battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_(crime) "Battery (crime)"), [domestic violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") or [child abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_abuse "Child abuse"). Whether an instance of corporal punishment exceeds these bounds is usually decided on a case-by-case basis in family court proceedings.

### Zimbabwe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Child_corporal_punishment_laws&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: Zimbabwe")]

In 2014, the High Court of Harare ruled that corporal punishment violated the [Constitution of Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Zimbabwe "Constitution of Zimbabwe") in all settings, with the Court calling for the Constitutional Court to confirm its decision.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-118) In 2017, Zimbabwe's High Court ruled that child corporal punishment in both the home and at school was unconstitutional, however, the Constitutional Court has not confirmed this judgement.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-120)

Article 241 of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act 2004 authorises “moderate corporal punishment” of children by parents, guardians and schoolteachers; article 7 of the Children's Act 1972 confirms the right of parents and guardians to “administer reasonable punishment”.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-121)

The **legality of corporal punishment of children** varies by country. [Corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_the_home "Corporal punishment in the home") of minor children by parents or adult guardians, which is intended to cause physical pain, has been traditionally legal in nearly all countries unless explicitly outlawed. According to a 2014 estimate by [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch"), "Ninety percent of the world's children live in countries where corporal punishment and other physical violence against children is still legal".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-HRW-1) Many countries' laws provide for a defence of "reasonable chastisement" against charges of assault and other crimes for parents using corporal punishment. This defence is ultimately derived from [English law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_law "English law").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-2) As of 2026, only one ([France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")) [permanent member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") along with three (adding [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan")) of seven [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") members and seven (adding [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") and [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea")) of the 20 [G20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G20 "G20") member states have banned the use of corporal punishment against children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-Gershoff2017-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-4)
